initial_requirements: USDA Agricultural Research Service needs a centralized system for watershed research data that is currently managed separately at individual sites. Watershed staff should upload and maintain standardized water, soil, land-management, conservation, and economic data, while researchers and approved public users can search, analyze, visualize, download, and report integrated datasets. Access must reflect the responsibilities and confidentiality limits of different user groups.

messages.content: Hello, I’m GPTREI, your requirements elicitation assistant. I’ll be gathering detailed information about the STEWARDS Agricultural Research Data System to make sure we understand the needs clearly and completely. Before we begin, are you in line with the scope of this interview, or do you have different expectations for what we should cover?

Yes, I’m aligned with that scope. We’re mainly looking to understand how the centralized watershed research data system should support data upload, maintenance, searching, analysis, visualization, downloads, reporting, and access control across different user groups.
To start off, could you please introduce yourself and your connection to this project?

I’m speaking as someone representing the watershed research data management side at ARS, so I’m familiar with the needs of the site staff and the researchers who use the data. My focus is on how STEWARDS can bring the separate site datasets into one system while still respecting the confidentiality and responsibilities tied to each user group.
Thank you. Could you describe the current process or systems the site teams use today to manage and share watershed research data?

Right now, the data is managed separately at individual research sites, and each site tends to have its own mix of spreadsheets, local databases, and shared folders or internal files. Sharing usually happens by emailing files, uploading them to site-specific locations, or sending extracts to researchers when needed, so it’s pretty fragmented and inconsistent.
What current processes do you want to change or improve, or what features do you hope to get from STEWARDS?

The biggest change we want is to stop the duplication and manual reformatting that happens when people move data between site systems and research users. We also want one place where standardized data can be uploaded, checked, and maintained, with search, visualization, download, and reporting tools built around the integrated datasets.

So far, I understand the main features as centralized standardized data upload and maintenance, data validation or checking, integrated search, visualization, download, reporting, and reducing duplication/manual reformatting across sites. Are there any other features you would like to see in this project?

It would also be helpful to have strong metadata support so users can understand what each dataset means, where it came from, and how it was collected. I’d also expect version history or audit trails for updates, since people will need to know what changed and when, especially for research use.
Based on your description, do you think role-based access control should also be included so that site staff, researchers, and approved public users only see and do what their permissions allow?

Yes, definitely. Access control has to reflect the different responsibilities and confidentiality limits, so site staff can manage their own data, researchers can work with approved datasets, and public users only see what’s cleared for release. We’d need that separation to be clear and enforced in the system.

Could you prioritize these features for me: standardized upload and maintenance, validation/checking, metadata support, version history/audit trails, search, visualization, download, reporting, and role-based access control?

Role-based access control is the top priority because everything else depends on getting permissions and confidentiality right. After that, standardized upload and maintenance and validation/checking come next, since the system has to get the data in correctly and consistently. Metadata support and version history are also very important, then search, reporting, visualization, and download, which are more about making the data usable once it’s in the system.
Please elaborate on what you want standardized upload and maintenance to accomplish.

We want site teams to be able to submit water, soil, land-management, conservation, and economic data in a consistent format without having to hand-convert everything first. The system should help keep the records aligned to shared standards, support updates when corrected data comes in, and avoid creating separate versions that drift apart across sites.
Could you describe more about how the system should handle validation or checking when those data are uploaded?

It should catch obvious problems at upload time, like missing required fields, bad date formats, values outside expected ranges, or records that don’t match the expected site or project structure. I’d want it to flag issues clearly so staff can correct them before the data is accepted, but I don’t think every warning has to block upload if it’s something the team can review later.
Could you describe more about the metadata support you need, especially what users should be able to see or record about each dataset?

Users should be able to record the basics like who collected the data, the site, the time period, the methods used, and any related project or treatment information. On the viewing side, people should be able to see enough context to understand whether the dataset fits their research needs and how it should be interpreted, without having to go back to the original site staff for every detail.
Could you describe more about the version history or audit trail you need, especially what changes should be tracked and who should be able to view that history?

We’d want to track who changed a record, when they changed it, and what was changed, especially for corrected measurements or metadata updates. Researchers and authorized staff should be able to view that history, but I wouldn’t expect the general public to need the full audit trail unless it’s tied to a released dataset summary.
Could you describe more about the search capability you need, especially how users should find datasets or records in the system?

Users should be able to search by site, date range, watershed, data type, and maybe project or treatment, since those are the ways people usually think about the data. It should also support filtering so they can narrow down to just the datasets they actually need, rather than getting a huge mixed list back.
Could you describe more about the reporting capability you need, especially what kinds of outputs or summaries users should be able to generate?

Reporting should let users produce summaries that combine data across sites or time periods, like basic trends, totals, or comparison tables for a watershed or project. Staff may also need more operational reports, such as what data has been loaded, what is missing, or where there are quality issues, while researchers will probably want exportable results they can use in presentations or publications.
Could you describe more about the visualization capability you need, especially what kinds of charts, maps, or views would be most useful?

Maps would be important for showing where sites are and how measurements vary by location, and time-series charts would be useful for seeing change over time in things like water quality or soil conditions. Some simple comparison views across treatments or sites would also help, but I wouldn’t expect anything overly fancy if it makes the system harder to use.
Could you describe more about the download capability you need, especially who should be able to download data and in what formats?

Researchers and approved public users should be able to download the data they’re allowed to see, while staff should be able to download broader working datasets for management and analysis. Common formats like CSV would be the most useful, and for some cases we’d probably want spreadsheet or geospatial formats too, but the exact list could depend on the data type.
Who else do you think has valuable insights into the project, and whose needs need to be considered, and why?

Definitely the watershed site staff, because they know the real collection and maintenance workflow and what data is practical to capture. Researchers are another key group since they need the data to be consistent, discoverable, and usable for analysis, and we also need to consider public users because some data will be shared more broadly. I’d also include data managers or administrators, since they’ll be responsible for oversight, permissions, and keeping the system organized over time.
What would you consider a successful deployment of STEWARDS?

A successful deployment would be one where the site staff actually use it to manage their watershed data instead of keeping separate local versions, and researchers can find and use integrated datasets without a lot of manual cleanup. It would also mean the access controls are working correctly, the data is reliable, and people trust the system enough to use it as the central source.

To summarize, we discussed a centralized watershed research data system for ARS that supports standardized upload and maintenance of water, soil, land-management, conservation, and economic data; validation at upload; strong metadata; version history/audit trails; search; reporting; visualization; download; and strict role-based access control for site staff, researchers, and approved public users. Success means staff actually use STEWARDS as the central source, researchers can access integrated datasets with less manual cleanup, and permissions/confidentiality are enforced correctly.

Is there anything else you would like to add?

One thing I’d add is that we’ll need the system to be easy enough for site staff to use consistently, because if the upload and maintenance process is too cumbersome, people will work around it. I’d also want good support for data quality issues, like flagging missing or suspicious values, so problems are caught early instead of after the data has been published or used in analysis.
